cards.front: Recall a key point about Tawhid: The Oneness of God
cards.back: Tawhid is the central belief of Islam — there is only one God (Allah), with no partners, equals or divisions. It is the first part of the Shahadah: "There is no god but Allah." Surah 112 (Al-Ikhlas) expresses tawhid: "He is Allah, the One and Only."

cards.front: Recall a key point about Tawhid: The Oneness of God
cards.back: Tawhid influences every aspect of Muslim life: it forbids shirk (associating partners with God), which is the greatest sin in Islam. This is why Muslims reject the Christian Trinity (they see it as shirk) and why images of Allah or Muhammad are forbidden in mosques (to prevent idolatry).

cards.back: 1. For Tawhid: The Oneness of God questions, always include specific scriptural or source references where relevant 2. Explain both religious and non-religious viewpoints 3. cards.front: What should you know about uk context?
cards.back: The Qur’an describes Allah’s creative power: “He it is who has created the heavens and the earth in six days and His Throne was upon the waters” (Surah 11:7). For Muslims, the natural world — its beauty, complexity and order — is evidence of Allah’s existence and power, inspiring gratitude and worship.

cards.front: What should you know about uk context?
cards.back: The destruction of the Buddhas of Bamiyan by the Taliban in 2001 was justified by some Muslims as opposition to shirk (idol worship). However, the vast majority of Muslim scholars condemned the destruction, arguing that Islamic law does not require the destruction of other people’s religious symbols and that tolerance of other faiths is a Qur’anic principle.

cards.front: What should you know about uk context?
cards.back: British Muslim athletes such as Mo Farah have spoken about how tawhid motivates their discipline and dedication. Farah has described his running career as an expression of gratitude to Allah for the talent he has been given, and he performs sujud (prostration) in gratitude after winning races.

Students often confuse Sunni and Shi'a beliefs about predestination. Wrong: "All Muslims believe everything is predestined and humans have no free will." Correct: "Most Muslims believe God has foreknowledge but humans have free will to choose; the balance between predestination and free will is understood differently across traditions."
